progress.resume_behavior: Resume each course at its first incomplete step.
progress.completion_behavior: A step is complete only after the learner chooses Continue or Finish.

safety.dirty_document_default: Keep the current document and its unsaved changes.

tutorials.title: Create your first Figure
tutorials.summary: Learn the Figure workspace by creating, naming, arranging, saving, and exporting a small scientific canvas.
tutorials.outcome: A named .fsfigure file containing a title, shape, scientific asset, and reviewed SVG export.

steps.title: Choose the Figure workspace
steps.instruction: Use the Figure | Presentation switcher and choose Figure. Confirm that the canvas, Figure tools, and Figure tab strip are visible.
steps.why: The workspace switcher changes the active tab collection without closing Presentation documents.
steps.callout: The Figure side of the switcher is selected and any Presentation tabs remain available when you switch back.

steps.title: Open a new Figure tab
steps.instruction: Choose New Figure, select a landscape preset, and create the document. Leave any other Figure tabs open.
steps.why: Every tab owns its own model, file path, dirty state, history, selection, and export target.
steps.callout: The new tab is named Untitled Figure followed by a number; existing tabs are unchanged.

steps.title: Add a title and shape
steps.instruction: Create a short live-text title, draw one rounded rectangle, and use the Properties controls to set a clear fill and stroke.
steps.why: Text, shapes, and appearance controls form the shared authoring foundation for both workspaces.
steps.callout: The active tab shows a dirty marker after the first document change.

steps.title: Insert a scientific asset
steps.instruction: Open Assets, search for cell, review the preview, and insert one released asset onto the artboard.
steps.why: The bundled library works offline and inserts editable vector artwork rather than a repository-linked placeholder.
steps.callout: The selected asset shows editable parts and Source & notes information.

steps.title: Arrange the canvas
steps.instruction: Select the shape and asset, align their vertical centers, then use arrow keys for a small final adjustment.
steps.why: Alignment gives repeatable geometry while direct nudging keeps deliberate visual judgment in the loop.
steps.callout: Only the selected objects move; content in other tabs is untouched.

steps.title: Save with a real filename
steps.instruction: Choose Save and give the .fsfigure file a descriptive name. In the desktop app, choose a folder in Save As; in a browser, keep the downloaded file.
steps.why: A saved .fsfigure file preserves the editable Figure for later revisions.
steps.callout: The confirmation identifies the filename. Desktop saves also show the chosen folder; browser downloads leave the destination to the browser.

steps.title: Export an SVG
steps.instruction: Choose Export As, select SVG, confirm the active Figure name and artboard scope, and export to a known folder.
steps.why: SVG preserves supported vector content and does not use a raster DPI setting.
steps.callout: The export status names this Figure, SVG, and the output filename; no other tab is exported.

tutorials.title: Build your first four-panel figure
tutorials.summary: Create a publication-ready four-panel Figure with consistent gutters, labels, imported results, layers, and deliberate exports.
prerequisites: Complete Create your first Figure or know the basic canvas tools
tutorials.outcome: A saved four-panel Figure with A–D labels, structured layers, reviewed imported content, and publication-resolution outputs.

steps.title: Create the four-panel document
steps.instruction: In the Figure workspace, choose New Figure and the four-panel manuscript layout. Create it as another tab.
steps.why: A dedicated tab keeps the tutorial Figure independent from every other open document.
steps.callout: Four editable panel frames and A–D labels appear on one Figure artboard.

steps.title: Name the source document
steps.instruction: Save the active Figure tab as an .fsfigure file before importing results. Use a project-specific filename.
steps.why: The editable document—not an exported image—is the source of truth for later revisions.
steps.callout: The confirmation identifies the filename. Desktop saves also show the chosen folder; browser downloads leave the destination to the browser.

steps.title: Set equal panel geometry
steps.instruction: Select the panel frames by row, align their tops, and distribute horizontal gaps. Repeat by column for vertical spacing.
steps.why: Explicit alignment and distribution make gutters repeatable without flattening the panels.
steps.callout: The four frames remain individually editable and stay inside the artboard.

steps.title: Place representative results
steps.instruction: Import an SVG or PDF result into one panel and a raster image into another. Review placement instead of stretching either source blindly.
steps.why: Vector and raster sources have different editing and resolution boundaries.
steps.callout: Imported artwork remains selected after placement and Source & notes identifies its origin.

steps.title: Complete the scientific story
steps.instruction: Add concise panel headings, assign title, annotation, and legend/body roles to the relevant live text, then choose Type > Publication typography and review the publisher-neutral profile before applying it.
steps.why: Role-aware named styles keep final-size scientific typography consistent without changing the measured result, notation, or panel geometry.
steps.callout: Review possible reflow, overset, font substitution, and the spatial A–D label sequence before applying one reversible document change.

steps.title: Organize layers and groups
steps.instruction: Name Results, Diagrams, Labels, and Annotations layers. Group each panel's artwork without hiding the A–D label structure.
steps.why: A readable object tree prevents accidental edits as scientific figures become dense.
steps.callout: Moving one panel group does not disturb unrelated panels.

steps.title: Check and export the Figure
steps.instruction: Run Figure check, resolve meaningful warnings, then export a 300 DPI PNG and a PDF. Open both outputs for a visual review.
steps.why: The final files—not only the live canvas—must preserve legibility, geometry, and intended resolution.
steps.callout: Raster settings appear for PNG but not PDF; export status names only the active Figure.

tutorials.title: Create an asset-based scientific diagram
tutorials.summary: Build a compact biological mechanism from released assets, attached connectors, labels, reusable styles, and an accessible legend.
prerequisites: Know how to create a Figure tab
tutorials.outcome: A saved biological mechanism diagram whose assets, labels, colors, and connectors remain editable.

steps.title: Write the diagram's message
steps.instruction: Add one sentence outside the artboard describing the relationship the finished diagram must communicate, then use it as an authoring check.
steps.why: A declared message helps distinguish meaningful visual structure from decoration.
steps.callout: The sentence is a working note and can be removed before export.

steps.title: Search by scientific concept
steps.instruction: Search the offline Asset Library for two or three concepts relevant to the mechanism. Compare available drawing styles before insertion.
steps.why: Concept-first search avoids treating alternate styles as unrelated scientific objects.
steps.callout: The library reports concepts and styles separately and shows Source & notes for released assets.

steps.title: Insert and arrange the actors
steps.instruction: Insert the chosen assets, scale them proportionally, and use alignment controls to establish a readable left-to-right or top-to-bottom flow.
steps.why: Stable spatial order lets readers infer sequence without relying on connector crossings.
steps.callout: Asset parts remain editable and no item leaves the artboard.

steps.title: Connect biological relationships
steps.instruction: Use Smart Connector to attach activation, inhibition, or transport relationships to meaningful endpoints. Label ambiguous connections with a short verb.
steps.why: Attached connectors preserve meaning when assets move and make the relationship type explicit.
steps.callout: Moving either endpoint reroutes the line without detaching it.

steps.title: Create a restrained visual system
steps.instruction: Use swatches or Recolor Selection to coordinate the diagram. Save a repeated label or callout appearance as a Graphic Style.
steps.why: A small reusable style system improves consistency without erasing semantic distinctions.
steps.callout: Color is reinforced with labels, arrowheads, line styles, or patterns where meaning depends on it.

steps.title: Review sources and accessibility
steps.instruction: Open Source & notes for each asset, then review labels, contrast, reading order, and line distinctions at the intended display size.
steps.why: Source information and accessible encoding belong in the review, not as afterthoughts.
steps.callout: The final diagram remains understandable without color alone.

steps.title: Save and export the diagram
steps.instruction: Save the editable Figure as an .fsfigure file, then export SVG for supported vector reuse and PNG at the actual delivery resolution.
steps.why: Keeping the editable source and reviewing both vector and raster outputs protects future revisions.
steps.callout: Each export reports this document, its format, and its destination.

tutorials.title: Edit vectors, paths, and nodes
tutorials.summary: Practice Selection and Direct Selection, Pen editing, node handles, compound paths, fills, strokes, gradients, and safe expansion.
prerequisites: Know how to select and move ordinary objects
tutorials.outcome: A saved vector study containing edited nodes, a compound shape, gradient appearance, and a reviewed expanded copy.

steps.title: Draw overlapping base shapes
steps.instruction: Draw an ellipse, rectangle, and freeform path with the Pen tool. Give each a visible fill and stroke.
steps.why: Simple overlapping geometry makes selection levels and path operations easy to see.
steps.callout: Selection shows object bounds; Direct Selection reveals path points and handles.

steps.title: Edit anchor points and handles
steps.instruction: Switch to Direct Selection, move one anchor, adjust a Bézier handle, and convert one point between corner and smooth behavior.
steps.why: Node editing changes path geometry without transforming the entire object.
steps.callout: Only the chosen node or handle moves, and Undo reverses the edit as one history step.

steps.title: Join and cut a path
steps.instruction: Cut one path at a deliberate point, inspect its endpoints, then join compatible endpoints. Undo and redo to verify the topology change.
steps.why: Topology commands alter connectivity and deserve an explicit review, not only a visual glance.
steps.callout: Open and closed path state is reflected in the node controls.

steps.title: Create a compound result
steps.instruction: Duplicate the base shapes, then apply one live Boolean or compound-path operation. Keep the originals nearby for comparison.
steps.why: A preserved source copy makes destructive expansion or topology changes easier to evaluate and reverse deliberately.
steps.callout: The live result remains editable until you explicitly expand it.

steps.title: Build a layered appearance
steps.instruction: Add a gradient fill and a second stroke, then reorder the appearance entries and adjust opacity on one entry.
steps.why: The appearance stack separates visual styling from path geometry.
steps.callout: The object remains one path while the inspector lists multiple appearance entries.

steps.title: Review masks and expansion
steps.instruction: Create a clipping example, duplicate it, and expand only the duplicate. Compare editability and appearance before keeping either result.
steps.why: Expansion trades live structure for paths and should never silently replace the editable source.
steps.callout: The original live object remains intact beside the expanded copy.

steps.title: Save the editable study
steps.instruction: Save the Figure as an .fsfigure file and export SVG. Reopen the .fsfigure file later when you need the full editable structure.
steps.why: An SVG export is not a substitute for the .fsfigure file's editable objects and supported live structures.
steps.callout: Save targets the active vector-study tab only.

tutorials.title: Work with imported SVG and PDF artwork
tutorials.summary: Open and place representative SVG and PDF content, review editability, protect source appearance, and make bounded vector or text changes.
prerequisites: Have a representative SVG and PDF available
Save important source files before editing

start.label: Keep current documents and open artwork deliberately

tutorials.outcome: A saved .fsfigure file with reviewed imported artwork, explicit protected content, and a visually checked PDF or SVG export.

steps.title: Protect current work first
steps.instruction: Review every dirty tab. Save the tabs you intend to keep before opening or importing external artwork.
steps.why: Open and Import have different destinations, and neither should put unrelated unsaved work at risk.
steps.callout: Dirty markers identify exactly which tabs still differ from their saved files.

steps.title: Open SVG as a new Figure
steps.instruction: Choose Open PDF or SVG, select a representative SVG, and let Figure Tool open it in a new Figure tab sized to the artwork.
steps.why: Open creates a new document; Import places content into the current document.
steps.callout: The previous active tab remains open and unchanged.

steps.title: Inspect SVG structure
steps.instruction: Use Selection, Direct Selection, and Layers to identify editable paths, text, groups, clips, and any protected effects.
steps.why: SVG is a container format; individual constructs can have different safe editing boundaries.
steps.callout: Protected content is labeled rather than silently flattened or omitted.

steps.title: Open a PDF page
steps.instruction: Open a representative PDF in another Figure tab. Compare the visible page with the source before editing.
steps.why: The source appearance is the baseline for judging any bounded PDF conversion or edit.
steps.callout: Source & notes keeps the original PDF relationship available.

steps.title: Make one bounded PDF edit
steps.instruction: Enter supported content with Direct Selection. Change one path or explicitly convert one detected text run while keeping outlines available.
steps.why: PDF text and effects often require font, spacing, mask, or blend review after conversion.
steps.callout: Unsupported structures remain protected and the original appearance is still reviewable.

steps.title: Save a Figure Tool copy
steps.instruction: Use Save As and choose a new Figure Tool filename. Do not overwrite the original SVG or PDF source.
steps.why: The .fsfigure file preserves supported edit structure and source notes separately from the imported file.
steps.callout: The active tab adopts the new .fsfigure filename. Desktop Save returns to the chosen path; browser Save downloads another copy.

steps.title: Export and compare
steps.instruction: Export PDF or SVG from the active imported-artwork tab and compare text, masks, gradients, line widths, and clipping with the source.
steps.why: A bounded edit is complete only after the intended output passes a visual comparison.
steps.callout: Figure Tool makes no claim of arbitrary PDF rewriting or universal Illustrator equivalence.

tutorials.title: Prepare a Figure for publication export
tutorials.summary: Choose physical size, resolution, format, artboard scope, background, and review steps for a publication-ready Figure.
prerequisites: Have a finished Figure tab available
Know the target journal or delivery requirements
tutorials.outcome: A saved source Figure plus one reviewed vector output and one correctly sized raster output.

steps.title: Confirm the active source tab
steps.instruction: Select the intended Figure tab, read its filename and dirty marker, and save it before creating delivery files.
steps.why: Save and Export apply only to the active tab; choosing the correct source is the first export decision.
steps.callout: No document in the Presentation workspace is affected.

steps.title: Translate delivery requirements
steps.instruction: Record the required physical size, pixel dimensions or DPI, color/background expectation, allowed formats, and whether the current or all artboards are needed.
steps.why: DPI is meaningful only with physical size or pixel dimensions and should not be guessed from the live canvas zoom.
steps.callout: Vector SVG and PDF controls do not show meaningless DPI settings.

steps.title: Run Figure check
steps.instruction: Review missing artwork, low-resolution images, overset text, unsupported appearance, and content outside the selected artboard scope.
steps.why: The check identifies likely delivery problems without rewriting scientific content.
steps.callout: Warnings remain ordinary, actionable language and can be reviewed before export.

steps.title: Export the vector delivery file
steps.instruction: Choose SVG or PDF according to the destination, set current or all artboard scope where available, and export without a DPI control.
steps.why: Vector outputs preserve supported paths and text or provide a portable publication page.
steps.callout: The status message identifies the Figure, format, and exact destination.

steps.title: Export the raster delivery file
steps.instruction: Choose PNG, JPEG, or TIFF, set 96, 150, 300, or 600 DPI—or explicit dimensions—and choose background or transparency only where the format supports it.
steps.why: Resolution and background settings determine raster suitability at the final physical size.
steps.callout: JPEG uses an opaque background; PNG and TIFF expose transparency only when supported.

steps.title: Inspect at final size
steps.instruction: Open both outputs in an independent viewer and inspect line weights, type, symbols, gradients, transparency, clipping, and raster sharpness at the intended size.
steps.why: Successful export does not guarantee that a file meets visual or publication requirements.
steps.callout: Keep the editable Figure Tool source after the delivery files are accepted.

tutorials.title: Build your first scientific presentation
tutorials.summary: Create a short deck with title, mechanism, result, and conclusion slides, then add notes, test playback, save, and export.
tutorials.outcome: A saved four-slide scientific Presentation with notes, tested playback, PDF output, and editable source content.

steps.title: Switch to the Presentation workspace
steps.instruction: Choose Presentation in the Figure | Presentation switcher and confirm that the slide navigator and Presentation tab strip appear.
steps.why: Presentation is a first-class deck workspace; Present or Slideshow is a command inside it.
steps.callout: Your Figure tabs remain open and return when you switch back.

steps.title: Create a widescreen deck
steps.instruction: Choose New Presentation, select 16:9, and choose a quiet scientific theme. Create it as a new Presentation tab.
steps.why: One deck size and theme establish a coherent starting system without changing other open decks.
steps.callout: The tab is named Untitled Presentation followed by a number and shows a dirty marker after edits.

steps.title: Author the title slide
steps.instruction: Apply a title layout, replace placeholders with a concise title and context line, and review readability at Fit Slide.
steps.why: A layout is an editable starting structure, not a locked template.
steps.callout: The complete slide fits inside the editor without hiding workspace controls.

steps.title: Add the scientific story
steps.instruction: Create mechanism, result, and conclusion slides. Use Duplicate where structure repeats, then replace the duplicated content deliberately.
steps.why: A short ordered story is easier to review than a collection of unrelated canvases.
steps.callout: The navigator lists four slides in title, mechanism, result, conclusion order.

steps.title: Add assets and results
steps.instruction: Insert an editable scientific asset on the mechanism slide and place a result SVG, PDF, PNG, or JPEG on the result slide. Add a take-home statement to each.
steps.why: The shared engine keeps scientific assets, imported artwork, shapes, connectors, and text editable in decks.
steps.callout: Edits belong to the active slide and active Presentation tab only.

steps.title: Add speaker notes
steps.instruction: Add one or two plain-text notes to each content slide. Keep detailed context or citations in notes instead of crowding the visible slide.
steps.why: Notes stay with their slide, reopen with the deck, and can participate in the bounded PPTX notes subset.
steps.callout: Changing slides changes the active note field without moving notes between slides.

steps.title: Save and test playback
steps.instruction: Save the active Presentation with a real filename, then Present from beginning and advance through every slide before exiting.
steps.why: Playback catches scale, overflow, sequence, and navigation issues before export.
steps.callout: The complete slide fits the stage and navigation, notes, and Exit remain reachable.

steps.title: Export the deck as PDF
steps.instruction: Choose Export As, select Presentation PDF and all slides, export to a known folder, then inspect every page in order.
steps.why: PDF is the dependable visual share for a scientific deck.
steps.callout: Export status names this Presentation, PDF, all slides, and the destination.

tutorials.title: Use slide layouts and themes
tutorials.summary: Build a coherent scientific deck with editable layouts, theme choices, slide-specific overrides, reordering, duplication, and notes.
prerequisites: Have a Presentation tab with at least three slides
tutorials.outcome: A coherent deck whose layouts, theme, slide-specific overrides, ordering, and notes have been reviewed in playback.

steps.title: Review the current theme
steps.instruction: Inspect the deck's theme colors, type choices, background, and layout defaults before applying changes.
steps.why: A theme is a coordinated starting system and should not erase intentional scientific distinctions.
steps.callout: Custom artwork remains editable and visible when the theme changes.

steps.title: Apply purpose-fit layouts
steps.instruction: Use different layouts for a title, comparison, result, and conclusion slide. Replace placeholder content with live text and artwork.
steps.why: Layouts provide repeatable structure while each slide remains independently editable.
steps.callout: Applying a layout does not flatten existing vector or image objects.

steps.title: Review typography after layout changes
steps.instruction: Check title length, body wrapping, hierarchy, contrast, and overset text on every changed slide at Fit Slide.
steps.why: Theme and layout changes can alter exact text wrapping even when content remains editable.
steps.callout: No text is clipped or too small at the intended playback size.

steps.title: Keep deliberate slide overrides
steps.instruction: Make one slide-specific color or type override that communicates meaning, then verify it remains distinct after another theme review.
steps.why: Scientific emphasis can require intentional exceptions to the deck-wide theme.
steps.callout: The override is local to the selected slide object.

steps.title: Exercise the slide navigator
steps.instruction: Duplicate one slide, move it to a new position, then delete only the duplicate. Confirm notes and content follow the intended original slide.
steps.why: Navigator operations define playback and export order and must remain scoped to this deck.
steps.callout: No slide in another Presentation tab changes.

steps.title: Review the system in playback
steps.instruction: Present from the current slide and inspect scale, hierarchy, repeated positions, contrast, and slide order through the deck.
steps.why: A coherent editor view can still reveal rhythm or fit problems during playback.
steps.callout: Every full slide fits, and Exit and navigation remain reachable.

steps.title: Save the deck state
steps.instruction: Save the active Presentation and wait for confirmation that identifies its .fsdeck filename.
steps.why: The saved .fsdeck file preserves slide order, size, theme, layouts, notes, and editable artwork.
steps.callout: The dirty marker clears only on this Presentation tab.

tutorials.title: Use the supported PPTX interchange subset
tutorials.summary: Import and export common scientific slide content through the bounded PPTX v1 subset and review every compatibility warning honestly.

start.label: Keep current documents and open a PPTX as another Presentation

tutorials.outcome: A reviewed Figure Tool Presentation and a destination-tested PPTX produced within the documented v1 subset.

steps.title: Read the compatibility boundary
steps.instruction: Open the PPTX compatibility article and identify supported, approximated, and unsupported constructs before import.
steps.why: PPTX is bounded interchange, not a promise of universal PowerPoint or Google Slides round-trip fidelity.
steps.callout: Google Slides compatibility is through common files, not direct cloud integration.

steps.title: Protect open documents
steps.instruction: Review dirty Presentation tabs and save the work you need before opening the representative PPTX in another tab.
steps.why: PPTX import should never replace unrelated work or save every open deck.
steps.callout: The current deck remains available after the imported deck becomes active.

steps.title: Open the representative PPTX
steps.instruction: Choose Open Presentation, select the PPTX, and review the import summary before editing any slide.
steps.why: The warning summary explains which objects remained editable, were approximated, flattened, or skipped.
steps.callout: The imported slide order and uniform slide size are visible in a new Presentation tab.

steps.title: Review every imported slide
steps.instruction: Inspect text wrapping, fonts, theme colors, shapes, connectors, images, speaker notes, and any labeled unsupported content.
steps.why: Editable common content can still render differently across applications and installed fonts.
steps.callout: SmartArt, charts, tables, media, animation, macros, OLE, 3D, and advanced masters are not silently treated as fully editable.

steps.title: Make a supported edit
steps.instruction: Change one plain text box, basic shape, line, connector, or embedded image and add one plain speaker note.
steps.why: A bounded edit exercises the subset without relying on unsupported PowerPoint-specific structures.
steps.callout: The edited object remains selectable and the deck shows a dirty marker.

steps.title: Save an editable Figure Tool source
steps.instruction: Use Save As to create an editable .fsdeck Presentation file before exporting another PPTX.
steps.why: The app-owned document is the durable source for Figure Tool state and supported future edits.
steps.callout: The original PPTX remains unchanged.

steps.title: Export and destination-test PPTX
steps.instruction: Export PPTX from the active deck, read every export warning, then open the file in PowerPoint or another PPTX consumer and review all slides and notes.
steps.why: Destination review is required because the v1 subset does not promise universal round-trip fidelity.
steps.callout: Export status names this Presentation, PPTX, and the output filename.

tutorials.title: Save, reopen, and recover documents safely
tutorials.summary: In the desktop app, practice Save and Save As for one .fsfigure or .fsdeck tab. Learn how .fsproject saves the open workspace and how browser downloads differ.
prerequisites: Have at least one Figure or Presentation tab with a small test edit

start.label: Use the active document without replacing it

tutorials.outcome: A verified current-format document, a separate Save As copy, a successful reopen, and a clear understanding of document versus project saving.

steps.title: Identify the exact save target
steps.instruction: Read the active workspace, active tab name, filename or untitled name, and dirty marker. Identify whether the active file will be .fsfigure or .fsdeck, and note another open tab that must remain unchanged.
steps.why: Save, Save As, and Export target only the active tab; Save Project is the separate command for an .fsproject workspace file.
steps.callout: Tabs in the other workspace are not part of this document save unless you explicitly choose Save Project.

steps.title: Use native Save As
steps.instruction: Choose Save As, select a known folder in the native dialog, enter a descriptive name, and save the active document.
steps.why: Save As always asks for a new path and never pretends a browser download has a known destination.
steps.callout: The success message states exactly what was saved and where in ordinary language.

steps.title: Verify later Save overwrites the same file
steps.instruction: Make a small edit, confirm the dirty marker, choose Save, and verify that no location dialog appears and the same file path is reported.
steps.why: A named tab owns one save target until Save As deliberately establishes another.
steps.callout: Only this tab's dirty marker clears.

steps.title: Create a separate copy
steps.instruction: Choose Save As again, save under a different name, then make another small edit and use Save.
steps.why: The active tab adopts the new path, while the first saved file remains a separate earlier copy.
steps.callout: The tab title changes to the new filename and later Save reports the new path.

steps.title: Reopen the saved document
steps.instruction: Open the first saved file as another tab and compare its expected content with the later Save As copy.
steps.why: A successful reopen is the practical proof that the saved document is durable and distinct.
steps.callout: Both files appear as separate tabs with independent histories and selections.

steps.title: Test the per-tab close guard
steps.instruction: Make one harmless edit in the reopened test tab, close only that tab, and choose Cancel when Figure Tool asks what to do with its unsaved changes.
steps.why: The close guard belongs to that document and must not save, discard, or close unrelated tabs.
steps.callout: Cancel returns to the exact dirty test tab and leaves every other document unchanged.

steps.title: Know browser fallback and recovery limits
steps.instruction: Read Save, reopen, and recovery Help. Confirm that .fsfigure and .fsdeck are individual documents, .fsproject contains the open workspace, and legacy .figurestudio files are import-only. In a browser, Save downloads a named file; it cannot report a folder path or overwrite an earlier download.
steps.why: Reliable recovery depends on deliberate current-format files and ordinary backups, not assumptions about hidden destinations or crash recovery.
steps.callout: Keep both test documents until reopening is verified; use Save Project separately when you need all open tabs in one file.
